text.string: Cross-sensor probabilistic identity tagging using a committee of experts

Every sensor learns the same set of prescribed attributes. The probability that a new observation has the same identity as a previous observation is defined by the distance between measurements of their real-world attributes
Two sensors of unrelated types can still agree on a target’s identity because they agree on what attributes it has in the real world.

Easy to implement

Good performance distinguishing substantially different targets

Different sensors reliably agree on identity

Most of the information sensors collect can’t contribute

Entire system is limited by the lowest-resolution sensor

Attributes are hand-picked

Every sensor is an expert on what attributes it can extract. Identity is expressed as two integers, coarse and fine. Broadly, the coarse score answers the question “what is this?” while the fine score answers “which one is this?” A deeper network learns how the attributes from each expert contribute to the coarse and fine scores, enabling each expert to find only the attributes that produce the strongest signal.
Identity is now a coordinate in a 2-dimensional latent space.
Two sensors can agree where a target belongs regardless of why.

props.text.string: This latent space is a projection of the much higher-order attribute spaces.

text.string: The latent space is mathematically unbounded, so it naturally contains objects it was never trained on, like this

What shape is a real object’s identity? In practice, identity will not be a discrete point. Inference will be noisy, and many points in a region will encode the same object. Moreover, I expect drift to be correlated with differences in observation angle at first. Understanding the geometry of those encoding regions will help me improve both the model and inference confidence accuracy.

Does identity inference decohere as objects become dissimilar to training data? Sensor experts learn to agree on the encodings for objects in their training data, but it’s not clear how closely those experts will continue to agree as they encounter objects that lack the features that are convenient in the training data.
